contentBlocks.content: Why compare mutual funds and ETFs?

Mutual funds and exchange-traded funds are both pooled investment vehicles. Both can hold collections of stocks, bonds, or other assets, and both can help investors gain exposure to many investments through one fund.

contentBlocks.title: The key idea
contentBlocks.content: The biggest differences are often in how the funds are structured, priced, traded, managed, and accessed. Neither structure is automatically better for every investor.
What is a mutual fund?

A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests that money according to the fund's stated strategy. Investors own shares or units of the fund rather than directly owning every underlying investment themselves.
What is an ETF?
An ETF is also a pooled investment fund, but its shares generally trade on an exchange during the trading day, similar to shares of an individual company.
Both can provide diversification
A mutual fund or ETF can hold many investments. This can make diversification easier than buying each investment separately.
But the fund's holdings still matter
Two funds can have completely different levels of diversification. One may hold thousands of companies, while another may focus on a small group of companies or a single industry.
How ETFs are traded

ETF shares generally trade on an exchange throughout the trading day. Their market price can change while the market is open based on supply, demand, and changes in the value of the underlying investments.
How mutual funds are priced

Mutual funds generally calculate a net asset value, or NAV, for their shares at a designated time, commonly at the end of the trading day. Investors typically transact based on that calculated NAV, subject to the fund's rules.

contentBlocks.title: Simple distinction
contentBlocks.content: ETF: generally trades throughout the day on an exchange. Mutual fund: generally transacts at a calculated NAV.
What is NAV?
Net asset value is the value of a fund's assets minus its liabilities, divided by the number of outstanding fund shares or units.
NAV per share = (fund assets − fund liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding

contentBlocks.title: Simple NAV calculation
contentBlocks.content: Suppose a fund has $10 million in assets, $200,000 in liabilities, and 980,000 shares outstanding. Its simplified NAV per share is approximately $10.
Active versus passive management

Both mutual funds and ETFs can be actively or passively managed. Active funds generally have managers selecting investments with the goal of achieving a particular objective, often outperforming a benchmark. Passive funds generally seek to track an index.
An ETF is not automatically passive
Many ETFs track indexes, but ETFs can also use active strategies. The word ETF tells you about the fund's structure and trading method, not necessarily whether it is active or passive.
A mutual fund is not automatically active
Mutual funds can also be designed to track indexes. Therefore, passive versus active is a separate question from ETF versus mutual fund.
Fees matter

Funds have costs. These can include operating expenses and, depending on the fund and platform, other charges. Investors should look at the actual fee structure rather than assuming one type of fund is always cheaper.
Expense ratio
The expense ratio expresses a fund's annual operating expenses as a percentage of its assets.

contentBlocks.title: Comparing fund costs
contentBlocks.content: If you have $25,000 invested in a fund with a 0.20% expense ratio, the simple annual cost represented by that ratio is about $50. At 1.00%, it would be about $250, ignoring changes in account value and other factors.
Trading costs can be different from fund expenses

The expense ratio is not the only potential cost. An ETF investor may also face trading-related costs depending on the brokerage and transaction. Mutual funds can have their own fees or transaction rules. Always check the actual fund and account terms.
Minimum investment requirements
Some mutual funds may have minimum investment requirements, while ETFs can generally be purchased according to the brokerage's trading rules and available share or fractional-share options.
Automatic investing
Some investors value the ability to automatically contribute a fixed amount to a fund on a recurring schedule. Whether this is easy or available depends on the brokerage and fund platform.
Liquidity

ETF shares generally trade throughout the day, but the ease and cost of trading can vary by ETF. Mutual funds generally do not trade like stocks during the day. Liquidity should therefore be considered alongside the specific fund and market.
Taxes can differ

The tax treatment of ETFs and mutual funds depends on the country, account type, fund structure, and investor circumstances. Investors should not assume that one structure always produces lower taxes.
What about index funds?
An index fund is defined by its strategy of tracking an index. It can be structured as an ETF or as a mutual fund. This means you can have an index ETF and an index mutual fund.

contentBlocks.title: Three different descriptions
contentBlocks.content: Fund A is an ETF that tracks a broad stock index. Fund B is a mutual fund that tracks the same type of index. Fund C is an actively managed mutual fund where a manager selects stocks. All three are funds, but their structures and strategies differ.
When an ETF may be attractive
An ETF may appeal to investors who value intraday trading, broad selection, transparency, or a particular low-cost passive strategy. The specific fund still needs to be evaluated.
When a mutual fund may be attractive

A mutual fund may appeal to investors who value automated contributions, professional management, particular fund strategies, or a platform that makes mutual-fund investing convenient. Again, the specific fund matters more than the label alone.
Neither structure guarantees better returns
ETF versus mutual fund is not a simple ranking. Investment results depend heavily on what the fund owns, its strategy, costs, market conditions, taxes, and investor behavior.
Common misconceptions
Misconception: Every ETF is an index fund
Reality: Many ETFs track indexes, but some ETFs are actively managed or follow other strategies.
Misconception: Every mutual fund is actively managed
Reality: Mutual funds can also passively track indexes.
Misconception: ETFs are always cheaper
Reality: Costs depend on the specific fund, strategy, fees, and trading arrangements.
Misconception: A lower share price means a cheaper fund
Reality: The share price does not tell you whether the fund is better value. What matters is the assets, strategy, costs, performance, and risks represented by the investment.
Misconception: ETFs and mutual funds cannot both be diversified
Reality: Both structures can provide broad diversification, depending on their holdings.
Practical decision framework

contentBlocks.title: Compare the actual fund, not just the label
contentBlocks.content: Check what it owns. Check whether it is active or passive. Identify its benchmark if applicable. Compare expense ratios and other costs. Consider how it trades. Check diversification and concentration. Consider tax implications in your country and account. Finally, ask whether the fund fits your investment goal and time horizon.
Practical calculation

contentBlocks.title: Why fees can create a meaningful difference
contentBlocks.content: Suppose two otherwise similar funds each have $40,000 invested. Fund A has a 0.15% expense ratio and Fund B has a 0.75% expense ratio. The simple annual difference represented by those expense ratios is $240.
$300 − $60 = $240 difference per year
The bigger lesson
Do not choose an investment merely because it is called an ETF or a mutual fund. Understand the fund underneath the label. The structure, strategy, holdings, costs, risks, and suitability all matter.

Mutual funds and ETFs are both pooled investment vehicles. ETFs generally trade throughout the day on exchanges, while mutual funds generally transact at a calculated NAV. Both can be active or passive and both can provide diversification. The best choice depends on the specific fund, costs, strategy, holdings, risks, taxes, and the investor's goals.

contentBlocks.title: Remember
contentBlocks.content: ETF versus mutual fund is a structure question. Active versus passive is a strategy question. Keep those two ideas separate.

quiz.question: What is one major difference between ETFs and mutual funds?
options: ETFs generally trade throughout the day on an exchange, while mutual funds generally transact at a calculated NAV
Only mutual funds can hold bonds
quiz.explanation: ETFs generally trade throughout the day, while mutual funds generally transact at a calculated NAV.

quiz.question: What does NAV stand for?
quiz.explanation: NAV stands for Net Asset Value.

quiz.question: A fund has $10 million in assets, $200,000 in liabilities, and 980,000 shares. What is its simplified NAV per share?
Every ETF is passively managed.
quiz.explanation: Some ETFs are actively managed, so ETF structure and investment strategy are separate concepts.

quiz.question: Can a mutual fund be an index fund?
options: Only if it trades on an exchange
Only if it owns one stock
quiz.explanation: A mutual fund can be designed to track an index.

quiz.question: What does an expense ratio represent?
options: The fund's annual operating expenses expressed as a percentage of assets
The number of stocks in the fund
quiz.explanation: An expense ratio expresses annual operating expenses as a percentage of the fund's assets.

quiz.question: Two funds each have $25,000 invested. Fund A has a 0.20% expense ratio and Fund B has a 1.00% expense ratio. What is the simple annual difference represented by those ratios?
quiz.explanation: Fund A represents $50 and Fund B represents $250, giving a $200 difference.

quiz.question: Which statement is most accurate?
options: ETF versus mutual fund tells you whether the fund is active or passive
ETF and mutual fund describe fund structures, while active and passive describe investment strategies
quiz.explanation: Fund structure and investment strategy are separate concepts.

quiz.question: Why shouldn't an investor choose a fund based only on its expense ratio?
options: The fund's holdings, strategy, risks, taxes, tracking, and suitability also matter
Higher fees always produce higher returns
Expense ratios determine the fund's share price
quiz.explanation: Costs matter, but they are only one part of evaluating an investment.

quiz.question: What is the best general approach when comparing an ETF and a mutual fund?
options: Choose whichever has the lower share price
Choose the one with the most impressive name
Compare the actual funds' holdings, strategy, costs, risks, taxes, and suitability
quiz.explanation: The specific investment matters more than the label alone.
